name: Comet's Toll

stars.name: Toll A
stars.notes: The steadier of the system's two orange dwarfs, holding a wide orbit around its companion; its relatively calm weather makes the inner mining lanes navigable at all.

stars.name: Toll B
stars.notes: A flare-prone red dwarf whose tantrums drive the comet stream's electrical activity; miners watch its light-curve the way sailors watch the barometer.

planets.name: Kiln
planets.notes: A tidally tortured rock squeezed between the binary's pulls; its constant quakes are used as a natural seismic clock by the inner mines.

planets.name: Grindstone
planets.notes: An airless crater-world hosting the system's main ore processing; its surface is black with tailings and lit orange by both suns at once.

planets.name: Ferryman's Rest
planets.notes: A marginal rock with sealed habitats for mine crews between rotations; nobody stays longer than contract requires, and the contract is short.

planets.name: Cold Ledger
planets.notes: The outer anchor of the settled system and the last safe harbor before the stream; ships register here before crossing into comet country.

anomalies.name: The Singing Ice
anomalies.notes: When Toll B flares, the stream's icy bodies discharge in cascading arcs that light up the dark like a burning fence. Beautiful from Cold Ledger. Fatal inside. Every miner has a story about hearing it through the hull.

asteroid_belts.name: The Toll Stream
asteroid_belts.location: crossing orbits 4-5 on an inclined plane
asteroid_belts.notes: Not a belt but a migrating river of comets herded by the binary's combined pull, crossing the shipping lanes twice per cycle. It holds the richest volatile deposits in the sector and exacts a price in hulls for every cargo taken.

stations.name: Pike Station
stations.notes: The largest of the ice camps: a hollowed comet-body with docking galleries, refinery stacks, and a chapel where the names of ships lost to the stream are carved into the ice wall.

stations.name: Ledger Light
stations.notes: The system's port of registry: insurance offices, salvage brokers, and the stream-forecasters whose daily predictions decide whether anyone crosses.

faction_control.notes: No authority can police the stream itself. Claims are staked, sold, jumped, and fought over along its whole length; Cold Ledger enforces order only within sight of its lights, and everyone knows it.

history: The stream was first worked by independent ice-riggers who established the claim customs still in use; half the sector's mining law descends from rules written in Pike Station's galley.

The Toll War, forty years past, began over a rich comet-body claimed by three crews simultaneously and ended with two burned hulls and one unchanged custom: possession during a Toll B flare lull is nine-tenths of the law.
Last cycle the stream shifted course early, catching twelve ships mid-crossing; nine made it to Cold Ledger, and the forecasters have been arguing about the new model ever since.
description: Two small stars, one orange and steady, one red and temperamental, wheel around each other while a river of comets threads between their worlds. The Toll Stream is not scenery: it is a moving mountain range of ice crossing the shipping lanes twice each cycle, glittering, dangerous, and full of money. From Cold Ledger's lights it looks like a frozen galaxy spilled across the dark.

Everything here serves the harvest. Miners ride the stream's margins for water, carbon, and rare ices; Grindstone processes what they bring back; Ledger Light sells forecasts, insurance, and quiet drinks to people who have just seen the Singing Ice up close. Traffic is moderate and hard-bitten, dominated by tugs, riggers, and salvage ships that follow the mining fleet like gulls.

The toll is real. The stream takes hulls every cycle, and the chapel wall at Pike Station grows by a few names a year. But the deeper unease is newer: since the stream changed course early last cycle, the old forecasting models fail more often than they hold, as if the river were learning to mislead them. The riggers have started leaving offerings again, an old custom from the first crews. Nobody laughs at it anymore.
